We study counterexample-guided synthesis of Riemannian contraction metrics for continuous-time autonomous systems on compact domains. A learner proposes a metric; a sound verifier certifies its matrix inequality or returns diagnostic points for retraining. The neural extension pairs a learned metric factor with symbolic contraction conditions and rigorous numerical verification; main ablations use fixed polynomial features. We give computable polynomial bounds in arbitrary dimension and implement outward-rounded verification for polynomial, trigonometric, and neural representations. Soundness of the numerical loop is separated from conditional finite-grid termination under idealized feasibility assumptions. We analyze why scaling and fixed-margin training can leave valid metrics uncertified. The scaling construction requires a scale-closed family, which the fixed-floor experimental class generally lacks. Verified positive slack improves the differential contraction rate and quantifies model-error tolerances using certified residual and Jacobian bounds. Finite-distance conclusions require a flowing connecting family that stays in the verified region. Experiments include controlled ablations, adaptive three-dimensional verification, and transfer from a trajectory-fitted surrogate with known-truth residual certification. In matched polynomial operating-grid experiments, trace normalization and margin coupling did not demonstrate an advantage in certification counts within the tested budgets. These choices address specific failure mechanisms without guaranteeing optimizer convergence or general empirical superiority.
